track.rule: Every step builds only on steps before it. tools/build.py fails the build if one doesn't.

stages.label: Week 1
stages.title: Data structures first
stages.goal: Hash maps, stacks, queues, trees and heaps feel routine at medium level, and you know what every operation costs.
stages.daily: Two timed problems a day from the chapters you have read, 25 minutes each, by the method in the algorithmic round chapter: say the brute force and its cost first, then improve it, then test it by hand before you run it. Log each one.

steps.do: Read it on day 1, before your first timed drill: it's the method for every drill and mock. Reread it the day before each coding mock.
Write your project deep dive, plus a 60-second answer to “tell me about yourself”. Recruiter and hiring manager screens open with these.
Read it, make the one-page cheat sheet in exercise 3, then do py_toolkit. Keep the cheat sheet next to you for every drill this week.
Read it and answer each quick check, then do the exercises. Save subarray_sum_count for week 2, after the two-pointers chapter: it needs prefix sums.

Read the Netflix culture memo, and Anthropic's mission, Core Views on AI Safety and Responsible Scaling Policy. Write a 90-second “why Netflix” and “why Anthropic”, each tying two of their values to something you did. In every recruiter call, ask for the screen's format and the onsite round list.
Ask Claude: “mock interview, past-project deep dive, 45 minutes”. Expect a follow-up on every choice: why this design, what broke, what you'd change.

stages.dayNote: About 33 hours. Times include each drill (25 minutes plus logging). Stretch exercises are optional this week. If a day runs long, move a drill to the next day rather than skip testing by hand. If you finish early, redo any drill you needed a hint for.

milestone.title: Mock 1: algorithmic coding
milestone.bar: One medium solved, tested by hand and explained in 45 minutes, with a 3 or better on problem solving and communication.

stages.label: Week 2
stages.title: Search, graphs and code built in levels; design starts
stages.goal: Binary search, two pointers and graph traversals are routine, you can build a component in levels with tests first, and you can size a system on paper.
stages.daily: Two timed problems a day, mixing this week's patterns with last week's. Once you've read the estimation chapter, add one back-of-envelope estimate a day: users, then requests per second, then storage.

steps.do: Ask Claude: “teach me testing for interviews” (45 minutes): which cases to write first, edge cases, and when a fake beats a mock. From now on, write three tests before you run any solution.
Ask Claude: “teach me designing for change” (45 minutes): small classes with one job, composition over inheritance, and adding a requirement without a rewrite.
Read it, then do token_bucket and rate_window_counter, the two an interviewer expects. The other two exercises are a stretch.
Two builds in levels, 90 minutes each, tests first: a key-value store with TTL and transactions, then an in-memory file system with sizes. Skip parking lot and elevator.
Ask Claude: “teach me requirements gathering” (30 minutes). Then open every design the same way: the features, the scale numbers, and what you will leave out.
Ask Claude: “mock interview, hiring manager round, 45 minutes”. Bring your deep dive, an ownership story and your “why this company”.

milestone.title: Mock 2: practical screen
milestone.bar: A problem in four levels in 90 minutes, each level adding a requirement. Levels 1 to 3 pass your own tests, no level forces a rewrite of the one before, and you score a 3 or better on code quality and on testing.
milestone.ask: mock interview, practical coding, 4 levels, 90 minutes

stages.label: Week 3
stages.title: Recursion and DP; how a request travels; coding with AI
stages.goal: Dynamic programming stops feeling like magic, you can trace a request from DNS to response and say what each hop costs, and you can steer an AI assistant and check its work.
stages.daily: Two timed problems a day, one of them from an earlier week, plus the daily estimate. Review beats new material once a pattern has faded.

steps.do: Read it, then do bit_tricks. The other two exercises are a stretch. Tries, sketches and consistent hashing use its shifts and masks later.
Read it, then do lru_cache and ttl_cache. lfu_cache is a stretch. Section 11 previews week 7's locks, so skim it.
Read it, then do interval_merge and interval_sweep. Skip interval_tree for now.
Sections 5, 9 and 10 of the estimation chapter cover most of it. Ask Claude to quiz you on the numbers, then explain p99 under fan-out back.
Sections 3 and 4 of the estimation chapter are the method. Ask Claude for three prompts and size each one out loud in under five minutes.

Ask Claude: “teach me TCP, HTTP, TLS and DNS”, one 60-minute session for this step and the next: handshakes and what they cost, keep-alive and connection reuse, HTTP/2 multiplexing, TLS termination. Skip congestion-control internals.
Covered in the same session as TCP vs UDP. Then explain back, hop by hop, what happens when a browser loads a page.
Ask Claude: “teach me systematic debugging” (30 minutes): reproduce, shrink the input, test one hypothesis at a time, bisect, and prove the fix with a test.

milestone.title: Mock 3: algorithmic screen
milestone.bar: Two mediums in 45 minutes, both tested by hand, with a 3 or better on all four coding signals. Pass this and Mock 2, and you are ready for technical screens.
milestone.ask: mock interview, coding, phone screen with two mediums, 45 minutes

stages.label: Week 4
stages.title: Load balancers, APIs, caches and databases; the first design
stages.goal: You can put a load balancer, an API and a cache in front of a database you chose and can defend, and you've done one design under time.
stages.daily: One timed problem a day, alternating between an algorithmic problem and one level of a practical build. Do each design as a 45-minute timed run, out loud, on the worksheet.

steps.do: Ask Claude: “teach me stateless services and load balancing”, one session for this step and the next: where session state lives and why that lets you add servers, then L4 vs L7, the balancing algorithms and health checks.
Covered in the same session as stateless services. Then explain back when you'd pick L4, when L7, and why sticky sessions hurt.
Ask Claude: “teach me SQL for interviews” (45 minutes). Then write five queries by hand: two joins, a GROUP BY with HAVING, a window function, and read one EXPLAIN.
Read it. Skip the three builds until after onsites.
Read it through “B-tree or LSM tree?”. Skip bplus_tree, lsm_store and wal_log until after onsites.
Ask Claude: “teach me data modeling and indexes”, one session for this step and the next: normalize first, denormalize for a query you can name, then which index serves which query.
Covered in the same session as data modeling. Then explain back how to order a composite index's columns, and when a covering index never touches the table.

Ask Claude: “teach me choosing a database” (30 minutes). Make a one-page table: relational, document, key-value, wide-column and search, each with the access pattern it fits and the reason you'd reject it.

milestone.title: Mock 4: AI-assisted coding
milestone.bar: A small component built with an AI assistant in 60 minutes while you narrate: context first, small steps, tests before trusting any output. You catch at least one wrong suggestion and say how you caught it.
milestone.ask: mock interview, AI-assisted coding round, 60 minutes

stages.label: Week 5
stages.title: Sharding, replication and queues
stages.goal: You can shard and replicate without hand-waving, say what consistency each read gets, and use a queue without losing or doubling messages.
stages.daily: One timed problem a day, alternating algorithmic and practical, plus one design run every other day.

steps.do: Read it, then do consistent_hash. Jump and rendezvous hashing are a stretch.
Ask Claude: “teach me consistency models and CAP”, one session for this step and the next.
Covered in the same session as consistency models. Then explain back what PACELC adds to CAP, with one real database on each side.
Ask Claude: “teach me message queues and delivery guarantees”, one session for this step and the next.
Covered in the same session as message queues. Then explain back how an idempotency key turns at-least-once delivery into effectively-once.
Ask Claude: “teach me SLIs, SLOs and error budgets” (45 minutes). From now on, end every design with your two SLOs and the one alert you'd page on.
Read it, then do dijkstra and its drills. Bellman-Ford and A* can wait.
Read it, then do greedy_intervals, gas_station and job_scheduling. Skip huffman_code.

milestone.title: Mock 5: system design
milestone.bar: A 3 or better on scoping and on the trade-offs in the deep dive, and a 2 or better on scale, failure and operations.

stages.label: Week 6
stages.title: Real-time delivery, ordering and the key-value store
stages.goal: Push delivery, clocks and quorums feel familiar, you know how systems fail, and the chat, key-value store and typeahead designs are done under time.
stages.daily: One timed problem a day, alternating algorithmic and practical, plus one design run every other day.

steps.do: Run this one as a scored mock. Ask Claude: “mock interview, system design, chat, 45 minutes”. Bar: a 3 or better on all four design signals, with one requirement changed at minute 25.
Read it, then do trie and trie_patterns. radix_tree is a stretch.

milestone.title: Mock 6: behavioral
milestone.bar: Every answer names your own actions and a measured result, with a 3 or better on ownership and on conflict. Include a story about candid feedback given and received (Netflix), and a specific answer on why Anthropic's mission matters to you.

stages.label: Week 7
stages.title: Concurrency, overload and the last designs
stages.goal: You can write thread-safe code and say why it is safe, you can keep a service up under overload, and the remaining classic designs are done.
stages.daily: One timed problem a day, every other one a concurrency problem, plus one design run every other day.

steps.do: Ask Claude: “teach me processes, threads and scheduling” (30 minutes): what a context switch costs, and what threads share that processes don't.
Ask Claude: “teach me threads, processes and asyncio” (60 minutes): the GIL, the event loop, gather, and a Semaphore to cap concurrency.
Practice for Mock 7: read it, then do striped_hash_map. The two lock-free exercises are a stretch.

Design it on a worksheet first (python3 tools/new.py case "Web crawler"), 45 minutes. Then code a small version: a pool of workers, a visited set and a per-host rate limit. Mock 7 is a variation of it.

milestone.title: Mock 7: concurrency coding
milestone.bar: A concurrent web crawler with a per-host rate limit in 45 minutes, with a test that would catch a race and a clear account of why it is safe.
milestone.ask: mock interview, concurrency coding: a concurrent web crawler with a per-host rate limit, 45 minutes

stages.label: Onsite
stages.title: Every round on your list, before the day
stages.goal: Start the day your first onsite is booked, wherever you are on the track. Ask the recruiter for the round list, rehearse only those formats, write any story you're missing, and run the full loop three or four days before.
stages.daily: One timed problem a day, and one mock every other day in the format you are weakest at.

steps.do: Ask Claude: “teach me reading unfamiliar code” (30 minutes): find the entry point, follow one request through, and write down the invariants. Then practice on a small open-source repository.
Only if your round list has a debugging round. Ask Claude: “mock interview, debugging round, 45 minutes”.
Only if your round list has a code review round. Ask Claude: “teach me reviewing a pull request” (30 minutes).
Only if your round list has a code review round. Ask Claude: “mock interview, code review round, 45 minutes”.
Only if your round list has a low-level design round. Ask Claude: “mock interview, object-oriented design, 45 minutes”.

milestone.title: Full loop rehearsal
milestone.bar: Coding, system design and behavioral back to back in one afternoon, each a 3 or better. Run it three or four days before the onsite.
milestone.ask: mock interview, full loop: coding, system design, behavioral

stages.label: Netflix
stages.title: Netflix pack
stages.goal: Start once a Netflix onsite is booked: their scale problems, their resilience habits and their culture. These designs build on replication and queues (week 5) and on failure handling (weeks 6 and 7). If the onsite is sooner, do those steps first, in track order.

steps.do: Ask Claude: “teach me deployment safety” (30 minutes): canary releases, feature flags and automatic rollback. Netflix asks how you ship safely, not only how you design.

stages.label: Anthropic
stages.title: Anthropic pack
stages.goal: Start once an Anthropic onsite is booked: serving models and building on them. These designs build on real-time delivery (week 6) and on retries, load shedding and the rate limiter (week 7). If the onsite is sooner, do those steps first, in track order.
